newsitem.title: UK: British trade unions demand new workplace rights.
newsitem.headline: British trade unions demand new workplace rights.

text.p: Britain's trade unions on Thursday rejected a call for the repeal of all the employment laws brought in by the Conservative government but backed a package of new rights for employees in the workplace.

The annual conference of the Trades Union Congress (TUC) backed a motion supporting a recent document from the opposition Labour Party called "Building Prosperity -- Flexibility, Efficiency and Fairness at Work".
The motion welcomed Labour's commitment to a national minimum wage and the proposed adoption of the Social Chapter of the Maastricht Treaty.

Labour will also outlaw discrimination against workers for belonging to a trade union and will make it a legal obligation for employers to recognise a union where a majority of the workforce vote for representation.
Labour will also scrap the "check-off" requirment -- one of the unions' biggest demands.
Under the "check-off" system, employers deduct union dues direct from an employee's wages and pass it on to the union.
A Conservative law requires the union to get a member's permission to do this every three years, which the unions say is costly and unnecessary.
The motion goes further than the Labour document, however, and Bill Morris of the Transport and General Workers Union, said it set out TUC priorities for the first year of any Labour government.
Tony Dubbins of the GPMU print union, and the incoming president of the TUC, highlighted four demands.
Firstly, he said "legally underwritten recognition" should be automatic where a trade union has more than 50 percent of the membership in any bargaining unit.
That recognition should cover all bargaining issues, including pensions and health and safety.
He argued that the requirement to ballot before recognition was granted would enable employers to manipulate the vote.
Secondly, he said Labour's proposal that workers sacked during a lawful dispute should be able to claim compensation for unfair dismissal was "helpful" but did not go far enough.
Wealthy employers were often only too willing to pay to get rid of trade union activists, he said.

"What we are looking for -- and indeed believe we have a just and moral case to insist upon -- is that any members engaged in a lawful dispute should have an automatic right to be reinstated when the dispute is over," Dubbins said.
Thirdly, the TUC wants the right to take solidarity action under certain circumstances, in line with International Labour Organisation conventions.

Dubbins highlighted the situation where, when a strike starts after a ballot, an employer transfers work to another plant. The TUC wants unionised members in this second plant to have the right to take solidarity action, something that is illegal under current legislation.
Finally, Dubbins said the unions wanted employment rights from day one of employment for all employees, including part- time and temporary workers.
Currently, a worker does not enjoy rights against dismissal and other rights until he or she has been in a particular job for two years.

There was no mention of this issue in Labour's recent policy document, and union leaders fear the party is reneging on a commitment given by former leader, the late John Smith, at the TUC conference in 1993.

The motion carried also called for limits on flexible hours contracts, and the banning of "zero hours" contracts under which an employee has no fixed working hours but can be called upon to work as and when an employer demands.
